Research/MD-COAS
Adaptive constraints

MD-COAS
Balance exploration, feasibility, and compute.

Hard constraints can reject most exploratory candidates, while soft penalties alone can leave unsafe solutions. MD-COAS brings both approaches into one model-based diffusion planner. A soft feasibility prior preserves informative guidance, a CFS projection corrects candidates, and adaptive scheduling decides how much constraint enforcement to apply as the trajectory distribution becomes cleaner. The result is a more flexible way to search highly non-convex environments under a computational budget.

Read the paperFigures & tablesRun this method

The question

How can a generative planner preserve useful exploration while enforcing difficult constraints, without spending the same correction effort at every denoising step?

Demonstrations

How it works

01

Keep imperfect samples informative

An inexact Augmented Lagrangian soft feasibility prior gives continuous weight to mildly infeasible candidates. Their constraint information can still guide the next update instead of disappearing behind a hard feasible-or-infeasible indicator.

02

Correct the full control sequence

A Convex Feasible Set projection constructs local constraint approximations and solves a structured quadratic program over the control sequence. Re-rolling the corrected controls through the dynamics preserves the connection between planned motion and the model.

03

Adapt enforcement during denoising

Constraint residuals adjust the soft-prior multipliers and penalties. A compute-aware primal–dual schedule also controls projection frequency, inner iterations, and active constraints, concentrating correction effort where it is needed.

Results

Paper results evaluate constraint optimization and adaptive scheduling on ten 2D difficulty levels and a 7-DoF arm obstacle-avoidance task.

Arm avoidance
100% safe success

Zero reported violations at all three tested obstacle radii; 5 random seeds and 20 trajectory candidates per seed at each level.

2D constrained maps
0.98–1.00 SSR

Safe & Success Rate reported in the result heatmap for Easy and Constrained map families, L1–L6. The more difficult non-convex Union Maps, L7–L10, achieve approximately 50% SSR.

Experimental protocol and metric definitions

± values are standard deviations, rendered from the original right-superscript notation. The paper reports no standard deviations for SSR or V.

The source table does not specify physical units for T, P, or obstacle radius; these are reproduced as reported.

CFS projection is applied to all unweighted trajectory samples. The paper reports a trade-off between planning performance and computation time.

Hardware: NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) and 9 CPU cores; CFS projections use jaxopt.

Table I · Paper ↗

Scope & trade-offs

Training-free single-robot planning with known dynamics, evaluated on randomized 2D obstacle maps and a D3IL 7-DoF arm avoidance task. The arm plans in joint space while its end-effector remains on a 2D workspace plane.

Full-sample CFS projection has a computational cost. MD-COAS is slower than MDOC in the reported 7-DoF table; adaptive scheduling improves efficiency relative to uniformly applied correction rather than guaranteeing a speedup over every baseline.

The hardest non-convex 2D maps remain challenging; the paper does not report universal success or safety across arbitrary environments.

This paper evaluates single-robot tasks. Richer dynamics and multi-robot coordination are future directions, not demonstrated extensions.

The next question

MD-COAS adapts how strongly and how often feasibility is enforced. 2GO asks how active constraint geometry can also shape the direction of refinement and the stochastic exploration itself, extending the story to constrained locomotion.
